title: The Fast Half of Strength
subtitle: Muscle power is the ability to produce force quickly. Here’s what that means in resistance training—and what the evidence does and doesn’t support.
imageAlt: Three adult family members share a strength-training space, each using a different level of support and resistance while a qualified trainer observes.
imageConcept: A warm, candid scene in a community strength studio: three adult family members of different ages work at nearby stations, one rising from a chair, another pressing a light resistance machine, and a third talking with a qualified trainer. The trainer offers guidance without a younger relative coaching anyone; the mood is collaborative, with each person adapting the movement to their own ability.
body:
A strength exercise is often described by how much resistance a person can move, or how many repetitions they can complete. There is another quality worth understanding: how quickly the body can produce force. Researchers call this muscle power. It matters in ordinary movement whenever the body needs to respond with purpose—standing up, stepping onto a curb, or moving an object without lingering under load.

Power is not simply speed, and it is not a demand to move recklessly. In resistance training, power-focused protocols commonly ask a person to lift the resistance with an intention to move quickly, then return it under control. The fast part is the effort, not a license to let momentum take over. The distinction gives strength training another lens, but it does not make every other form of training obsolete.

Imagine a seated leg press. A person using a power-oriented approach would press the platform away with a brisk, deliberate effort, then bend the knees and bring it back slowly enough to stay in control. The load should allow a clean movement; the goal is not to test a one-repetition maximum or make the machine move at any cost. With a chair stand, a similar idea might mean rising with a purposeful effort and sitting back down steadily, if that movement is appropriate for the person.

The controlled return is important because the whole repetition still needs to be manageable. If a person has to jerk, bounce, hold their breath, lose their balance, or shorten the movement to create speed, the setup is asking too much. “Fast” describes the intention during the lifting phase; it does not mean rushing the transition, skipping the return, or turning a set into a race.

Traditional strength training can also involve effortful lifting. Power training makes the intent to accelerate the resistance a deliberate feature, while adjusting the load and movement to keep the repetition safe and repeatable.
The evidence is promising, not settled

Research reviews do not establish power training as a universal upgrade. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials involving 566 community-living older adults found a modest advantage for power training on some physical-function measures compared with traditional strength training. The authors rated the evidence low certainty and called for larger, higher-quality studies. That caveat matters: the result is a reason to keep studying the approach, not a guarantee of extra benefit for an individual [1].

A separate 2023 review of 19 trials and 1,055 participants reached a more cautious overall conclusion: high-velocity power training and traditional resistance training had similar effects on functional performance, with uncertainty remaining for most outcomes [2]. Differences among study participants, programs, outcomes, and methods make a simple winner difficult to name.

Taken together, the reviews support a measured conclusion. Training with speed intent is a credible way researchers have studied resistance exercise, and it may help some people on some measures. The evidence does not show that everyone needs to train this way, that it prevents falls, or that it reliably produces better everyday function than conventional resistance work.
Why the question matters—and where it fits

The CDC emphasizes that people differ in their fitness, comfort, health conditions, and abilities. That framing is useful: activity should fit the person rather than assume one approach works for everyone [3].

Power is also one component of a broader approach to movement. CDC guidance for adults 65 and older includes aerobic, muscle-strengthening, and balance activities, with activities suited to a person’s fitness, comfort, health conditions, and abilities. A power-focused exercise, when appropriate, can sit inside that bigger picture; it is not a substitute for it [3].

It may help to think of power as a training question rather than a fitness identity. A person need not be an athlete, train explosively, or chase a performance number to ask whether a slightly more purposeful lifting effort belongs in their program.
How to explore it without turning it into a test

If you already do resistance exercise, begin with a conversation rather than adding speed on your own. Ask a qualified trainer or physical therapist whether power-focused movement makes sense for your goals, health, balance, joint comfort, and training experience. If you have a chronic condition, pain, recent surgery, or concerns about falling, discuss the appropriate type and amount of activity with a health professional before changing your routine.

Useful questions include: Which movement should I start with? What support or equipment would make it stable? How light should the resistance be while I learn the movement? What should the controlled return feel like? What are the signs that I should stop or adjust? Can you watch a few repetitions and help me distinguish purposeful speed from momentum?

A practitioner might choose a machine, a supported movement, or a familiar exercise before considering anything more demanding. The point is to make the exercise fit the person, not to make the person prove they can move quickly. If the movement causes pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness, or loss of control, stop and seek appropriate guidance.
What a well-adjusted repetition should look like

A practical first step, if a professional has cleared or recommended it, is to rehearse the movement without trying to make it fast. Learn the setup, range, breathing, and return. Then ask the professional to help select a resistance that allows a smooth, purposeful lifting effort without straining. A load that is light enough to control is not a failure; it may be the right place to learn.

During the effort, aim to move with intention while keeping the movement’s path steady. Return the resistance at a pace you can control. Rest between repetitions or sets as advised, and stop before fatigue changes the quality of the movement. The appropriate number of repetitions, sets, and sessions depends on the individual and the program; the research reviews do not provide a universal prescription for readers to copy.

If speed disappears, posture changes, or the return becomes a drop, pause and reassess with the person guiding the session. Progress might mean improving control or comfort before adding resistance or changing pace. Those decisions are more useful than trying to make every repetition faster.

The appeal of power training is not that it turns strength into a race. It draws attention to a quality that ordinary load-based descriptions can miss: how decisively a person can apply force. That can be a productive focus for a supervised program, especially when its goals and adaptations are chosen with the person doing the work.

But the current research leaves room for uncertainty, and that is not a reason to dismiss it—or to oversell it. Traditional resistance training remains a sound option. For someone curious about power, the next step is not maximal weights or improvised explosive movements; it is a specific conversation with a qualified professional about whether speed intent can be introduced safely, and how to keep the return controlled. Strength has more than one dimension, and training should make room for the whole person.
